opening.text: Have you ever missed a turn on a long drive? The road looks right. The sky is clear. But somewhere in the back of your mind you know something is off. Then the voice from the phone says, “Recalculating.” It does not scold you. It does not say you are a bad driver. It simply shows you a way back to the road you wanted.
That is a good picture of repentance. We all take wrong turns. The question is not whether we will. The question is what we do when we notice. Today I want to talk about the way back.

mainMessage.text: Repentance is not a punishment. It is a gift. Through Jesus Christ, we can turn around, be forgiven, and feel peace again. It asks us to change our minds and our hearts. And it is open to every one of us, no matter how far we have gone.

blocks.text: Let us begin with the first words the Savior taught when He started His ministry in Galilee.
From that time Jesus began to preach, and to say, Repent: for the kingdom of heaven is at hand.
This was His opening message. It was not a threat. It was an invitation to get ready for something good, the kingdom of heaven. Isaiah spoke of the same invitation centuries earlier.
Let the wicked forsake his way, and the unrighteous man his thoughts: and let him return unto the Lord, and he will have mercy upon him; and to our God, for he will abundantly pardon.
Notice two things. First, repentance reaches our “thoughts” as well as our actions. Second, God promises mercy, and He says He will “abundantly pardon.” That word, abundantly, means more than enough.
Elder Dallin H. Oaks of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles explained what repentance asks of us. In his talk “Repentance and Change,” from the October 2003 general conference, he said:

The gospel of Jesus Christ challenges us to change. ‘Repent’ is its most frequent message, and repenting means giving up all of our practices—personal, family, ethnic, and national—that are contrary to the commandments of God. The purpose of the gospel is to transform common creatures into celestial citizens, and that requires change.
So repentance is about change. It is more than feeling bad. It is turning the car around.
Peter taught the same thing to a crowd in Jerusalem after he had healed a man at the temple gate.
Repent ye therefore, and be converted, that your sins may be blotted out, when the times of refreshing shall come from the presence of the Lord;
Hear the promise inside that verse. Our sins can be “blotted out.” And times of refreshing come from the Lord’s presence. Repentance leads to relief.

If repentance is a gift, who paid for it? We could not turn back on our own strength. We needed help. The Lord Himself spoke about this in a revelation to Joseph Smith. He describes what He suffered for us.

These words are tender and heavy at the same time. The Savior suffered so that we would not have to carry the full weight of our sins. He asks only that we repent. That is why repentance is possible at all.
The prophet Samuel, a Lamanite, taught the Nephites how this works. He spoke about the Savior’s Atonement and what it makes possible.

Yea, and it bringeth to pass the condition of repentance, that whosoever repenteth the same is not hewn down and cast into the fire; but whosoever repenteth not is hewn down and cast into the fire; and there cometh upon them again a spiritual death, yea, a second death, for they are cut off again as to things pertaining to righteousness.
“The condition of repentance” is brought to pass by the Savior’s sacrifice. Without Him, there would be no road back. With Him, whosoever repents is not cut off.
Elder D. Todd Christofferson of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles testified of this. In his talk “The Divine Gift of Repentance,” from the October 2011 general conference, he said:

I gratefully acknowledge and testify that the incomprehensible suffering, death, and Resurrection of our Lord ‘bringeth to pass the condition of repentance’ (Helaman 14:18). The divine gift of repentance is the key to happiness here and hereafter. In the Savior’s words and in deep humility and love, I invite all to ‘repent: for the kingdom of heaven is at hand’ (Matthew 4:17). I know that in accepting this invitation, you will find joy both now and forever.
He calls it a divine gift. A gift is not earned. It is received. Our part is to say yes to it.
So what do we actually do? The Lord gave a clear answer in another revelation.

Behold, he who has repented of his sins, the same is forgiven, and I, the Lord, remember them no more.
By this ye may know if a man repenteth of his sins—behold, he will confess them and forsake them.

There are two actions here: confess and forsake. To confess is to admit what we did, first to God and, when needed, to those we have hurt. For some serious sins, it also means speaking with our bishop or branch president. To forsake is to stop and not go back.
The wise man Solomon wrote about what happens when we hide our wrongs.
He that covereth his sins shall not prosper: but whoso confesseth and forsaketh them shall have mercy.
Hiding does not help us. Honesty opens the door to mercy.
President Dieter F. Uchtdorf taught that this begins with faith. In his talk “Point of Safe Return,” from the April 2007 general conference, he said:

We need a strong faith in Christ to be able to repent. Our faith has to include a ‘correct idea of \[God’s\] character, perfections, and attributes’ (Lectures on Faith \[1985\], 38). If we believe that God knows all things, is loving, and is merciful, we will be able to put our trust in Him for our salvation without wavering. Faith in Christ will change our thoughts, beliefs, and behaviors that are not in harmony with God’s will.
That is a hopeful idea. We repent best when we believe that God is merciful. When we know He loves us, turning back does not feel like walking into a courtroom. It feels like walking toward home.
What happens when we do turn back? The scriptures describe it with beautiful pictures. Isaiah gave one that many of us know.
Come now, and let us reason together, saith the Lord: though your sins be as scarlet, they shall be as white as snow; though they be red like crimson, they shall be as wool.
Scarlet is a color that does not wash out. Yet the Lord says it can become white as snow. He is not asking us to pretend that nothing happened. He is promising to make us clean.

President Boyd K. Packer of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles spoke to people who feared they had gone too far. In his talk “The Brilliant Morning of Forgiveness,” from the October 1995 general conference, he said:

The gospel teaches us that relief from torment and guilt can be earned through repentance. Save for those few who defect to perdition after having known a fulness, there is no habit, no addiction, no rebellion, no transgression, no offense exempted from the promise of complete forgiveness.
No habit. No addiction. No rebellion. That list covers a lot of ground. If you have been afraid that your story is the exception, listen again to those words.
The people of King Benjamin knew this feeling. They had listened to his sermon and seen themselves clearly. Then they cried out to God.

And they had viewed themselves in their own carnal state, even less than the dust of the earth. And they all cried aloud with one voice, saying: O have mercy, and apply the atoning blood of Christ that we may receive forgiveness of our sins, and our hearts may be purified; for we believe in Jesus Christ, the Son of God, who created heaven and earth, and all things; who shall come down among the children of men.
And it came to pass that after they had spoken these words the Spirit of the Lord came upon them, and they were filled with joy, having received a remission of their sins, and having peace of conscience, because of the exceeding faith which they had in Jesus Christ who should come, according to the words which king Benjamin had spoken unto them.
Look at the order. They saw their need. They asked for mercy through the Savior. Then the Spirit came, joy followed, and they had “peace of conscience.” That is what forgiveness feels like.
Heaven also celebrates. The Savior told us so Himself.
I say unto you, that likewise joy shall be in heaven over one sinner that repenteth, more than over ninety and nine just persons, which need no repentance.
When you repent, someone is glad. There is joy in heaven. You are not coming back to a cold door.
Sometimes we feel bad but do not change. Paul explained the difference between two kinds of sorrow.
For godly sorrow worketh repentance to salvation not to be repented of: but the sorrow of the world worketh death.
Godly sorrow moves us toward God. It makes us want to do better. Worldly sorrow only wants to avoid the consequences. Mormon saw the second kind among his own people.

But behold this my joy was vain, for their sorrowing was not unto repentance, because of the goodness of God; but it was rather the sorrowing of the damned, because the Lord would not always suffer them to take happiness in sin.
Their sorrow was real, but it did not lead them to change. Sorrow that does not lead to change is not yet repentance.

And here is another honest truth. Even after we repent, we may not feel better right away. Some people turn back and then wonder, “Why do I still feel heavy?” Elder Neil L. Andersen of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles gave this counsel. In his talk “Repent … That I May Heal You,” from the October 2009 general conference, he said:
For those who are truly repentant but seem unable to feel relief: continue keeping the commandments. I promise you, relief will come in the timetable of the Lord. Healing also requires time.
A broken bone does not heal the moment the doctor sets it. Healing takes time. If you have done your part and still feel the weight, keep going. Relief will come.
There is one more thing to say. Repentance is never a thing to put off. Amulek taught the people of Ammonihah with great urgency.

And now, as I said unto you before, as ye have had so many witnesses, therefore, I beseech of you that ye do not procrastinate the day of your repentance until the end; for after this day of life, which is given us to prepare for eternity, behold, if we do not improve our time while in this life, then cometh the night of darkness wherein there can be no labor performed.
Amulek says, “do not procrastinate.” The best day to turn is today. A small turn now is easier than a big turn later.
Elder Jeffrey R. Holland of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles spoke to those who feel it is too late. In his talk “Prophets in the Land Again,” from the October 2006 general conference, he said:

To all of you who think you are lost or without hope, or who think you have done too much that was too wrong for too long, to every one of you who worry that you are stranded somewhere on the wintry plains of life and have wrecked your handcart in the process, this conference calls out Jehovah’s unrelenting refrain, ‘\[My\] hand is stretched out still’ \[see Isaiah 5:25; 9:17, 21\].
The hand is stretched out still. It has not been pulled back. Take it today.

story.prompt: The member tells a true time they turned back to God, or saw someone else do it. If the member has none, the app offers a story from the scriptures.
story.title: Alma the Younger

blocks.text: Alma was the son of a prophet, but he spent his young years working against the Church. Then an angel stopped him. For three days he could not speak or move, and he was racked with guilt over what he had done. In his own words, here is the moment it turned.

And it came to pass that as I was thus racked with torment, while I was harrowed up by the memory of my many sins, behold, I remembered also to have heard my father prophesy unto the people concerning the coming of one Jesus Christ, a Son of God, to atone for the sins of the world.
Now, as my mind caught hold upon this thought, I cried within my heart: O Jesus, thou Son of God, have mercy on me, who am in the gall of bitterness, and am encircled about by the everlasting chains of death.
And now, behold, when I thought this, I could remember my pains no more; yea, I was harrowed up by the memory of my sins no more.
And oh, what joy, and what marvelous light I did behold; yea, my soul was filled with joy as exceeding as was my pain!

He remembered what his father had taught about the Savior. He prayed one short prayer for mercy. And the weight lifted. His pain was replaced by joy. Alma went on to become a great prophet and teacher. That is what the Savior can do.

application.text: Here are three ways to act this week.
First, take a quiet moment and ask God, “Is there something I need to turn from?” Listen. Then write down what comes to mind.
Second, take one small step. If you owe someone an apology, give it. If a habit is pulling you down, take one concrete step away from it today.
Third, if the weight is heavy, speak with your bishop or branch president. He can help you find the way back, and he can help you carry what is too heavy to carry alone.
And if you are already on the road back, keep going. Healing takes time. But it comes.

closingVerse.text: The Lord is merciful and gracious, slow to anger, and plenteous in mercy. He will not always chide: neither will he keep his anger for ever. He hath not dealt with us after our sins; nor rewarded us according to our iniquities. For as the heaven is high above the earth, so great is his mercy toward them that fear him. As far as the east is from the west, so far hath he removed our transgressions from us.

opening.text: Every parent knows the moment. A child runs in from the yard, and there it is on a white shirt. A dark stain. Some stains come out with one wash. Others seem to stay forever. You scrub, you soak, and you wonder if the shirt is ruined.
Many of us feel that way about our own mistakes. We think the stain is too deep. We think it will always show. Today I want to share good news. There is One who can make us clean, and He wants to.

mainMessage.text: Repentance is how the Savior washes us clean. It takes honesty and a real change of heart. But the cleansing itself is His gift. He paid for it, and He offers it to everyone who comes to Him.

blocks.text: When Jesus Christ began teaching, He opened with one short sentence.
From that time Jesus began to preach, and to say, Repent: for the kingdom of heaven is at hand.
He started with repentance because it is the doorway. Before we can walk into the kingdom, we turn toward it. The prophet Isaiah described what that turning looks like.
Let the wicked forsake his way, and the unrighteous man his thoughts: and let him return unto the Lord, and he will have mercy upon him; and to our God, for he will abundantly pardon.

Isaiah says to forsake our way and our thoughts. That is a deep kind of change. And then comes the promise: mercy and abundant pardon. God does not give us the bare minimum. He gives more than we ask.
Elder Dallin H. Oaks of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles described the heart of this work. In his talk “Repentance and Change,” from the October 2003 general conference, he said:

The gospel of Jesus Christ challenges us to change. ‘Repent’ is its most frequent message, and repenting means giving up all of our practices—personal, family, ethnic, and national—that are contrary to the commandments of God. The purpose of the gospel is to transform common creatures into celestial citizens, and that requires change.
Think of the phrase “transform common creatures into celestial citizens.” That is a big goal. It is not about being slightly better. It is about becoming new.
The Apostle Peter taught this to the people of Jerusalem, and his words give us the order of things.
Repent ye therefore, and be converted, that your sins may be blotted out, when the times of refreshing shall come from the presence of the Lord;
First we repent. Then we are converted, which means changed at the core. Then our sins are blotted out. And times of refreshing follow. Like a clean shirt on a warm day, the relief is real.
We cannot scrub out our own stains. We do not have what it takes. So who pays the price? The Lord answered in a revelation given through Joseph Smith.
He suffered it so that we would not have to. He says, “if they would repent.” That small word, if, is our part. He did the heavy work. We choose to accept it.
Samuel the Lamanite taught the Nephites about this gift many years before the Savior was born.

Yea, and it bringeth to pass the condition of repentance, that whosoever repenteth the same is not hewn down and cast into the fire; but whosoever repenteth not is hewn down and cast into the fire; and there cometh upon them again a spiritual death, yea, a second death, for they are cut off again as to things pertaining to righteousness.
Samuel says the Savior “bringeth to pass the condition of repentance.” In other words, because of Him, repentance works. Without His sacrifice, it would be only good intentions.
Elder D. Todd Christofferson of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles called repentance a gift. In his talk “The Divine Gift of Repentance,” from the October 2011 general conference, he said:

I gratefully acknowledge and testify that the incomprehensible suffering, death, and Resurrection of our Lord ‘bringeth to pass the condition of repentance’ (Helaman 14:18). The divine gift of repentance is the key to happiness here and hereafter. In the Savior’s words and in deep humility and love, I invite all to ‘repent: for the kingdom of heaven is at hand’ (Matthew 4:17). I know that in accepting this invitation, you will find joy both now and forever.
Notice that he says “the key to happiness.” Not a burden. A key. It opens a door that nothing else can.
What is our part in the washing? The Lord named it plainly.

Behold, he who has repented of his sins, the same is forgiven, and I, the Lord, remember them no more.
By this ye may know if a man repenteth of his sins—behold, he will confess them and forsake them.

To confess is to say it out loud, to God first. If others were hurt, we make it right where we can. And if the sin is serious, we also speak with our bishop or branch president. To forsake is to leave it behind. Both are needed. And see the promise: the Lord says He will “remember them no more.”
Solomon wrote that hiding our mistakes never works.
He that covereth his sins shall not prosper: but whoso confesseth and forsaketh them shall have mercy.
A stain that is hidden is still a stain. Brought into the light, it can be cleaned.
President Dieter F. Uchtdorf taught that this work rests on trust in God. In his talk “Point of Safe Return,” from the April 2007 general conference, he said:

We need a strong faith in Christ to be able to repent. Our faith has to include a ‘correct idea of \[God’s\] character, perfections, and attributes’ (Lectures on Faith \[1985\], 38). If we believe that God knows all things, is loving, and is merciful, we will be able to put our trust in Him for our salvation without wavering. Faith in Christ will change our thoughts, beliefs, and behaviors that are not in harmony with God’s will.
When we believe God is kind, we stop hiding. We bring the stain to Him. And we find that He is not angry. He is ready to help.
When the washing is done, what do we find? The prophet Isaiah recorded the Lord’s own words.
Come now, and let us reason together, saith the Lord: though your sins be as scarlet, they shall be as white as snow; though they be red like crimson, they shall be as wool.

Scarlet and crimson are the hardest colors to remove. The Lord chose them on purpose. He is telling us that even the worst stains can be made white. And He opens with a kind invitation: “Come now, and let us reason together.” He is not shouting. He is inviting us to a conversation.

President Boyd K. Packer of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles gave a strong assurance to those who doubt. In his talk “The Brilliant Morning of Forgiveness,” from the October 1995 general conference, he said:

The gospel teaches us that relief from torment and guilt can be earned through repentance. Save for those few who defect to perdition after having known a fulness, there is no habit, no addiction, no rebellion, no transgression, no offense exempted from the promise of complete forgiveness.
The promise is complete. It does not come in parts. When we repent with real intent, we are not given a lesser kind of forgiveness.
Here is how it felt for a whole people. King Benjamin had finished his sermon, and the people looked at their own lives.

And they had viewed themselves in their own carnal state, even less than the dust of the earth. And they all cried aloud with one voice, saying: O have mercy, and apply the atoning blood of Christ that we may receive forgiveness of our sins, and our hearts may be purified; for we believe in Jesus Christ, the Son of God, who created heaven and earth, and all things; who shall come down among the children of men.
And it came to pass that after they had spoken these words the Spirit of the Lord came upon them, and they were filled with joy, having received a remission of their sins, and having peace of conscience, because of the exceeding faith which they had in Jesus Christ who should come, according to the words which king Benjamin had spoken unto them.
They asked for His blood to cleanse them. Then joy came, and so did “peace of conscience.” That quiet peace is one of the best signs that we have been forgiven.
And it is not a private event. The Savior said heaven itself rejoices.
I say unto you, that likewise joy shall be in heaven over one sinner that repenteth, more than over ninety and nine just persons, which need no repentance.
There is a party in heaven when one person turns back. That person might be you.
Not every kind of sadness leads to repentance. Paul separated them clearly.
For godly sorrow worketh repentance to salvation not to be repented of: but the sorrow of the world worketh death.
Godly sorrow says, “I hurt someone, and I want to make it right.” Worldly sorrow says, “I got caught, and I wish it had not cost me.” The first one leads to change. The second one leads nowhere.
Mormon watched a people who had only the second kind.

But behold this my joy was vain, for their sorrowing was not unto repentance, because of the goodness of God; but it was rather the sorrowing of the damned, because the Lord would not always suffer them to take happiness in sin.
They cried, but they did not turn. Tears without change do not wash anything.

Now let us speak of those who have turned. Sometimes the guilt lingers even after we have done everything right. Elder Neil L. Andersen of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles spoke to this. In his talk “Repent … That I May Heal You,” from the October 2009 general conference, he said:
For those who are truly repentant but seem unable to feel relief: continue keeping the commandments. I promise you, relief will come in the timetable of the Lord. Healing also requires time.
Do not give up when the feeling is slow to come. Keep doing what is right. The Lord has His own timing, and He keeps His promises.
Amulek spoke to people who thought they could put this off. His words still reach us.

And now, as I said unto you before, as ye have had so many witnesses, therefore, I beseech of you that ye do not procrastinate the day of your repentance until the end; for after this day of life, which is given us to prepare for eternity, behold, if we do not improve our time while in this life, then cometh the night of darkness wherein there can be no labor performed.
He pleads with them. “I beseech of you.” He knows how easy it is to say, “Later.” But a stain that sits for years is harder to clean. Today is better than tomorrow.

Elder Jeffrey R. Holland of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles offered hope to everyone who thinks they are too far gone. In his talk “Prophets in the Land Again,” from the October 2006 general conference, he said:

To all of you who think you are lost or without hope, or who think you have done too much that was too wrong for too long, to every one of you who worry that you are stranded somewhere on the wintry plains of life and have wrecked your handcart in the process, this conference calls out Jehovah’s unrelenting refrain, ‘\[My\] hand is stretched out still’ \[see Isaiah 5:25; 9:17, 21\].
No one is too far gone. The hand is still reaching.

story.prompt: The member tells about a time they were forgiven, or watched someone return. If the member has none, the app offers a story from the scriptures.
story.title: The prodigal son

blocks.text: The Savior told a story about a young man who left home and wasted everything he had. When he had nothing left, he made a decision.

And when he came to himself, he said, How many hired servants of my father’s have bread enough and to spare, and I perish with hunger!
I will arise and go to my father, and will say unto him, Father, I have sinned against heaven, and before thee,
And am no more worthy to be called thy son: make me as one of thy hired servants.
And he arose, and came to his father. But when he was yet a great way off, his father saw him, and had compassion, and ran, and fell on his neck, and kissed him.
And the son said unto him, Father, I have sinned against heaven, and in thy sight, and am no more worthy to be called thy son.
But the father said to his servants, Bring forth the best robe, and put it on him; and put a ring on his hand, and shoes on his feet:
And bring hither the fatted calf, and kill it; and let us eat, and be merry:
For this my son was dead, and is alive again; he was lost, and is found. And they began to be merry.

The young man planned a speech. But the father did not wait to hear it. He saw his son far away, ran to him, and embraced him. The best robe went on, and a feast was prepared. That is how our Heavenly Father receives us when we come home.

application.text: Here are three things to try this week.
First, name one thing you know you need to change. Be honest and specific. Then tell Heavenly Father about it in prayer.
Second, do one thing to make it right. Apologize, return what is not yours, or end the habit. Small steps count.
Third, if you carry something heavy, speak with your bishop or branch president. You do not need to carry it alone.
And remember that the feeling of peace may arrive slowly. Keep going. It is coming.

closingVerse.text: I, even I, am he that blotteth out thy transgressions for mine own sake, and will not remember thy sins.

opening.text: Imagine a boy who falls from a tree and breaks his arm. He could say, “It is fine,” and keep playing. But every time he lifts it, the pain gets worse. At some point he has to go to a doctor. The doctor does not shame him for falling. The doctor looks at the break, sets the bone, and tells him how to heal.

Sin is a little like that. We can pretend it is not there. But it hurts, and it does not heal on its own. The best thing we can do is bring it to the One who knows how to heal. That is what repentance is.

mainMessage.text: Repentance is the way to healing. It begins when we admit that something is broken. It continues as we turn to the Savior, confess, and change. And it ends in peace, because He has already paid for what we could not.

blocks.text: The first public words of the Savior’s ministry were about this.
From that time Jesus began to preach, and to say, Repent: for the kingdom of heaven is at hand.
He did not begin with rules or with warnings. He began by calling people to turn, because that is where all healing starts. Isaiah taught that God is eager to receive us when we do.
Let the wicked forsake his way, and the unrighteous man his thoughts: and let him return unto the Lord, and he will have mercy upon him; and to our God, for he will abundantly pardon.
“Let him return unto the Lord.” Return is a homecoming word. And God does not just tolerate our return. He will “abundantly pardon.”
Elder Dallin H. Oaks of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles taught what real repentance involves. In his talk “Repentance and Change,” from the October 2003 general conference, he said:

The gospel of Jesus Christ challenges us to change. ‘Repent’ is its most frequent message, and repenting means giving up all of our practices—personal, family, ethnic, and national—that are contrary to the commandments of God. The purpose of the gospel is to transform common creatures into celestial citizens, and that requires change.
The doctor can set the bone. But the boy still has to stop climbing that tree in the same way. Real repentance changes how we live.
Peter preached about this to a crowd in Jerusalem, and he said what comes after.
Repent ye therefore, and be converted, that your sins may be blotted out, when the times of refreshing shall come from the presence of the Lord;
The result is refreshing. When we turn, the Lord does more than forgive. He refreshes us. He brings new life into places that were tired and hurt.
Here is something every doctor in the world cannot do. No doctor can heal a soul. Only the Savior can, because He took our pain upon Himself. In a revelation to Joseph Smith, He described it.
The suffering He describes is beyond what we can picture. He did it for “all.” That includes you. And He says it was so we “might not suffer if they would repent.”
Samuel the Lamanite stood on a wall in Zarahemla and taught what this sacrifice makes possible.

Yea, and it bringeth to pass the condition of repentance, that whosoever repenteth the same is not hewn down and cast into the fire; but whosoever repenteth not is hewn down and cast into the fire; and there cometh upon them again a spiritual death, yea, a second death, for they are cut off again as to things pertaining to righteousness.
Because of the Savior, the condition of repentance exists. A door has been opened that would have stayed shut.
Elder D. Todd Christofferson of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles gave his witness. In his talk “The Divine Gift of Repentance,” from the October 2011 general conference, he said:

I gratefully acknowledge and testify that the incomprehensible suffering, death, and Resurrection of our Lord ‘bringeth to pass the condition of repentance’ (Helaman 14:18). The divine gift of repentance is the key to happiness here and hereafter. In the Savior’s words and in deep humility and love, I invite all to ‘repent: for the kingdom of heaven is at hand’ (Matthew 4:17). I know that in accepting this invitation, you will find joy both now and forever.
Notice that he says the Atonement is “incomprehensible.” We will never fully understand what it cost Him. But we can be deeply grateful, and we can accept His gift.
What does the Savior ask us to do? The Lord gave a simple test to know if we have repented.

Behold, he who has repented of his sins, the same is forgiven, and I, the Lord, remember them no more.
By this ye may know if a man repenteth of his sins—behold, he will confess them and forsake them.

Confess and forsake. Confession means we are honest about the wound. It starts with prayer to God. When others are involved, we make things right as best we can. For serious sins, we talk with our bishop or branch president, who is there to help us heal. Forsaking means we stop doing what hurt us.
Solomon wrote that a hidden wound does not help us.
He that covereth his sins shall not prosper: but whoso confesseth and forsaketh them shall have mercy.
The boy who hides his broken arm only prolongs the pain. Honesty brings mercy.
President Dieter F. Uchtdorf explained what makes this possible. In his talk “Point of Safe Return,” from the April 2007 general conference, he said:

We need a strong faith in Christ to be able to repent. Our faith has to include a ‘correct idea of \[God’s\] character, perfections, and attributes’ (Lectures on Faith \[1985\], 38). If we believe that God knows all things, is loving, and is merciful, we will be able to put our trust in Him for our salvation without wavering. Faith in Christ will change our thoughts, beliefs, and behaviors that are not in harmony with God’s will.
A patient who trusts the doctor follows the treatment. A person who trusts the Savior follows the path of repentance. Faith in His mercy makes the first step possible.
When a wound heals, the pain fades and the skin becomes whole. Forgiveness is like that. Isaiah gave us the Lord’s words about it.
Come now, and let us reason together, saith the Lord: though your sins be as scarlet, they shall be as white as snow; though they be red like crimson, they shall be as wool.
The Lord does not offer a rough patch. He offers white as snow. And the invitation is gentle: “Come now, and let us reason together.”

President Boyd K. Packer of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles testified that no one is beyond this healing. In his talk “The Brilliant Morning of Forgiveness,” from the October 1995 general conference, he said:

The gospel teaches us that relief from torment and guilt can be earned through repentance. Save for those few who defect to perdition after having known a fulness, there is no habit, no addiction, no rebellion, no transgression, no offense exempted from the promise of complete forgiveness.
He names the habits, the addictions, and the rebellion. He does not leave anything out. The promise covers it all.
The people of King Benjamin saw this healing happen to them in a single day.

And they had viewed themselves in their own carnal state, even less than the dust of the earth. And they all cried aloud with one voice, saying: O have mercy, and apply the atoning blood of Christ that we may receive forgiveness of our sins, and our hearts may be purified; for we believe in Jesus Christ, the Son of God, who created heaven and earth, and all things; who shall come down among the children of men.
And it came to pass that after they had spoken these words the Spirit of the Lord came upon them, and they were filled with joy, having received a remission of their sins, and having peace of conscience, because of the exceeding faith which they had in Jesus Christ who should come, according to the words which king Benjamin had spoken unto them.
A remission of sins. Peace of conscience. These are the signs of a healed soul. They are quiet, and they are real.
And the Savior told us that heaven welcomes us back.
I say unto you, that likewise joy shall be in heaven over one sinner that repenteth, more than over ninety and nine just persons, which need no repentance.
Heaven is glad when we repent. The recovery is not met with disappointment. It is met with joy.
Healing takes more than a moment, and Paul taught that the kind of sorrow we feel matters.
For godly sorrow worketh repentance to salvation not to be repented of: but the sorrow of the world worketh death.
Godly sorrow turns us toward the Healer. Worldly sorrow keeps us stuck in regret. Mormon saw a people who had the second kind.

But behold this my joy was vain, for their sorrowing was not unto repentance, because of the goodness of God; but it was rather the sorrowing of the damned, because the Lord would not always suffer them to take happiness in sin.

Their sorrow was real, but it did not make them better. If our sorrow only makes us feel worse, we may not yet be turning to the Savior. If it makes us want to change and to draw near to Him, it is the kind that heals.

Some people ask, “I have repented. Why do I still feel the weight?” Elder Neil L. Andersen of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles answered with care. In his talk “Repent … That I May Heal You,” from the October 2009 general conference, he said:
For those who are truly repentant but seem unable to feel relief: continue keeping the commandments. I promise you, relief will come in the timetable of the Lord. Healing also requires time.
A cast stays on for weeks. We do not take it off after one day and say it failed. Stay with the treatment. Relief is coming on His timetable.
No one who has a broken arm says, “I will see the doctor next year.” Amulek taught the same urgency about repentance.

And now, as I said unto you before, as ye have had so many witnesses, therefore, I beseech of you that ye do not procrastinate the day of your repentance until the end; for after this day of life, which is given us to prepare for eternity, behold, if we do not improve our time while in this life, then cometh the night of darkness wherein there can be no labor performed.
He asks us not to procrastinate. This life is the time to prepare. The sooner we begin, the sooner we heal.

Elder Jeffrey R. Holland of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles reached out to those who think they have missed their chance. In his talk “Prophets in the Land Again,” from the October 2006 general conference, he said:

To all of you who think you are lost or without hope, or who think you have done too much that was too wrong for too long, to every one of you who worry that you are stranded somewhere on the wintry plains of life and have wrecked your handcart in the process, this conference calls out Jehovah’s unrelenting refrain, ‘\[My\] hand is stretched out still’ \[see Isaiah 5:25; 9:17, 21\].
The hand is stretched out still. The Healer has not left the room.

story.title: Enos and his wrestle in prayer

blocks.text: Enos was the grandson of Lehi. He was a young man who went out to hunt, and while he was alone, his father’s teachings came back to his mind. Here is what he wrote.

And I will tell you of the wrestle which I had before God, before I received a remission of my sins.
Behold, I went to hunt beasts in the forests; and the words which I had often heard my father speak concerning eternal life, and the joy of the saints, sunk deep into my heart.
And my soul hungered; and I kneeled down before my Maker, and I cried unto him in mighty prayer and supplication for mine own soul; and all the day long did I cry unto him; yea, and when the night came I did still raise my voice high that it reached the heavens.
And there came a voice unto me, saying: Enos, thy sins are forgiven thee, and thou shalt be blessed.
And I, Enos, knew that God could not lie; wherefore, my guilt was swept away.

Enos did not rush. He prayed all day and into the night. Then the answer came, and his guilt was swept away. He called it a wrestle, and it was. But he did not stop praying until he received an answer.

application.text: Here are three ways to put this into practice.
First, set aside a quiet time to pray, as Enos did. Tell God what you need to turn from, and ask for His help.
Second, pick one thing you will stop doing, and one thing you will start doing. Keep it small and clear.
Third, if you are carrying something heavy, talk with your bishop or branch president. He is a servant of the Lord and can help you heal.
And be patient with yourself. A healing takes the time it takes.

opening.text: Picture a man who owes a large debt. He cannot pay it. Every month the weight grows. He lies awake at night, afraid of the knock on the door. Then one day a friend walks in, sits down, and says, “I have paid it all. You are free.”
The man would be stunned. He might even wonder if it was a trick. But the friend would only smile and hold out the receipt.
That is what the Savior has done for us. We owe a debt we could never pay. He paid it. And repentance is how we accept the receipt.

mainMessage.text: We all fall short, and none of us can fix that alone. Jesus Christ paid the price. Repentance is our way of saying yes to what He did. It means we turn, we confess, and we begin to live differently. And as we do, we are forgiven and set free.

blocks.text: When the Savior began to preach, He did not open with a long list. He gave one short call.
From that time Jesus began to preach, and to say, Repent: for the kingdom of heaven is at hand.
The kingdom is near. He is inviting us to turn and walk into it. Isaiah described the same invitation long before.
Let the wicked forsake his way, and the unrighteous man his thoughts: and let him return unto the Lord, and he will have mercy upon him; and to our God, for he will abundantly pardon.
Hear the generosity in that verse. A person returns, and God shows mercy. He does not haggle. He will “abundantly pardon.”
Elder Dallin H. Oaks of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles taught what this change looks like. In his talk “Repentance and Change,” from the October 2003 general conference, he said:

The gospel of Jesus Christ challenges us to change. ‘Repent’ is its most frequent message, and repenting means giving up all of our practices—personal, family, ethnic, and national—that are contrary to the commandments of God. The purpose of the gospel is to transform common creatures into celestial citizens, and that requires change.
The debt is paid, but we do not go back to the habits that created it. We change.
Peter taught the same thing at the temple in Jerusalem.
Repent ye therefore, and be converted, that your sins may be blotted out, when the times of refreshing shall come from the presence of the Lord;
“Blotted out” is a bookkeeping phrase. Think of a line drawn through a debt in a ledger. It is gone, and the account is clear.
Who paid? Not a bank. Not a stranger. The Lord Himself. In a revelation given through Joseph Smith, He said:
This was not a small payment. He trembled. He bled at every pore. And He finished it, for us. Through that sacrifice, we are given a way out.
Samuel the Lamanite taught the Nephites that this payment makes repentance possible.

Yea, and it bringeth to pass the condition of repentance, that whosoever repenteth the same is not hewn down and cast into the fire; but whosoever repenteth not is hewn down and cast into the fire; and there cometh upon them again a spiritual death, yea, a second death, for they are cut off again as to things pertaining to righteousness.
Because of the payment, the “condition of repentance” is in place. Without it, there would be no way to settle the account.
Elder D. Todd Christofferson of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles testified of this gift. In his talk “The Divine Gift of Repentance,” from the October 2011 general conference, he said:

I gratefully acknowledge and testify that the incomprehensible suffering, death, and Resurrection of our Lord ‘bringeth to pass the condition of repentance’ (Helaman 14:18). The divine gift of repentance is the key to happiness here and hereafter. In the Savior’s words and in deep humility and love, I invite all to ‘repent: for the kingdom of heaven is at hand’ (Matthew 4:17). I know that in accepting this invitation, you will find joy both now and forever.
He calls it a gift, and a key to happiness. When someone pays your debt, the right response is to say thank you and to receive it.
How do we accept what He offers? The Lord gave a clear sign of true repentance.

Behold, he who has repented of his sins, the same is forgiven, and I, the Lord, remember them no more.
By this ye may know if a man repenteth of his sins—behold, he will confess them and forsake them.

To confess is to admit the debt. We bring it before God in prayer. Where others were harmed, we try to make it right. If the sin is serious, we also meet with our bishop or branch president. To forsake is to stop adding to the debt. And then comes the line that should lift every heart: “I, the Lord, remember them no more.”
Solomon wrote about those who try to hide their debts.
He that covereth his sins shall not prosper: but whoso confesseth and forsaketh them shall have mercy.
Hiding keeps us stuck. Confessing leads to mercy.
President Dieter F. Uchtdorf taught what helps us come forward. In his talk “Point of Safe Return,” from the April 2007 general conference, he said:

We need a strong faith in Christ to be able to repent. Our faith has to include a ‘correct idea of \[God’s\] character, perfections, and attributes’ (Lectures on Faith \[1985\], 38). If we believe that God knows all things, is loving, and is merciful, we will be able to put our trust in Him for our salvation without wavering. Faith in Christ will change our thoughts, beliefs, and behaviors that are not in harmony with God’s will.
If we think the One who holds the account is harsh, we will avoid Him. But if we know He is loving and merciful, we come with confidence. That is why knowing who He is matters so much.
When a debt is cleared, a man can breathe again. The Lord used a picture to describe what happens to our sins.
Come now, and let us reason together, saith the Lord: though your sins be as scarlet, they shall be as white as snow; though they be red like crimson, they shall be as wool.
Scarlet is deep and strong. Snow is pure. The Lord says that the one can become the other. And He begins with a friendly call: “Come now.”

President Boyd K. Packer of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles spoke to people who feared their debt was too large. In his talk “The Brilliant Morning of Forgiveness,” from the October 1995 general conference, he said:

The gospel teaches us that relief from torment and guilt can be earned through repentance. Save for those few who defect to perdition after having known a fulness, there is no habit, no addiction, no rebellion, no transgression, no offense exempted from the promise of complete forgiveness.
The words “complete forgiveness” are worth holding on to. The Savior does not say, “I will pay half.” He says the account will be cleared.
The people who heard King Benjamin knew what it felt like to be forgiven. They had looked at their own lives and then asked for mercy.

And they had viewed themselves in their own carnal state, even less than the dust of the earth. And they all cried aloud with one voice, saying: O have mercy, and apply the atoning blood of Christ that we may receive forgiveness of our sins, and our hearts may be purified; for we believe in Jesus Christ, the Son of God, who created heaven and earth, and all things; who shall come down among the children of men.
And it came to pass that after they had spoken these words the Spirit of the Lord came upon them, and they were filled with joy, having received a remission of their sins, and having peace of conscience, because of the exceeding faith which they had in Jesus Christ who should come, according to the words which king Benjamin had spoken unto them.
They asked for His atoning blood to be applied. Then the Spirit came and filled them with joy. They had peace of conscience. The fear of the knock on the door was gone.
And the Savior said that heaven is glad.
I say unto you, that likewise joy shall be in heaven over one sinner that repenteth, more than over ninety and nine just persons, which need no repentance.
When one person turns back, there is joy in heaven. Our return matters to those who love us.
A man can feel bad about a debt without ever changing how he spends. Paul taught that there are two kinds of sorrow.
For godly sorrow worketh repentance to salvation not to be repented of: but the sorrow of the world worketh death.
Godly sorrow makes us want to change. The sorrow of the world just wishes it had not happened. Mormon saw a people with the second kind.

But behold this my joy was vain, for their sorrowing was not unto repentance, because of the goodness of God; but it was rather the sorrowing of the damned, because the Lord would not always suffer them to take happiness in sin.
Their tears did not lead to change. Sorrow that does not move us toward God is not yet repentance.

And even for those who have turned, the feelings of guilt can take time to fade. Elder Neil L. Andersen of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles gave a promise. In his talk “Repent … That I May Heal You,” from the October 2009 general conference, he said:
For those who are truly repentant but seem unable to feel relief: continue keeping the commandments. I promise you, relief will come in the timetable of the Lord. Healing also requires time.
If your debt is paid but you still feel afraid, trust the receipt. Keep the commandments. The relief will come.
Amulek taught that we have a season in which to settle our accounts.

And now, as I said unto you before, as ye have had so many witnesses, therefore, I beseech of you that ye do not procrastinate the day of your repentance until the end; for after this day of life, which is given us to prepare for eternity, behold, if we do not improve our time while in this life, then cometh the night of darkness wherein there can be no labor performed.
He calls this life the time “to prepare for eternity.” Each day we put it off is a day we carry what we could set down.

Elder Jeffrey R. Holland of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles reached out to anyone who feels they are beyond help. In his talk “Prophets in the Land Again,” from the October 2006 general conference, he said:

To all of you who think you are lost or without hope, or who think you have done too much that was too wrong for too long, to every one of you who worry that you are stranded somewhere on the wintry plains of life and have wrecked your handcart in the process, this conference calls out Jehovah’s unrelenting refrain, ‘\[My\] hand is stretched out still’ \[see Isaiah 5:25; 9:17, 21\].
He is still holding out the receipt. Take it.

story.title: The people of Nineveh

blocks.text: Jonah was sent to the great city of Nineveh to warn the people. He told them that the city would be overthrown in forty days. And something unusual happened. The people listened.

So the people of Nineveh believed God, and proclaimed a fast, and put on sackcloth, from the greatest of them even to the least of them.
For word came unto the king of Nineveh, and he arose from his throne, and he laid his robe from him, and covered him with sackcloth, and sat in ashes.
And he caused it to be proclaimed and published through Nineveh by the decree of the king and his nobles, saying, Let neither man nor beast, herd nor flock, taste any thing: let them not feed, nor drink water:
But let man and beast be covered with sackcloth, and cry mightily unto God: yea, let them turn every one from his evil way, and from the violence that is in their hands.
Who can tell if God will turn and repent, and turn away from his fierce anger, that we perish not?
And God saw their works, that they turned from their evil way; and God repented of the evil, that he had said that he would do unto them; and he did it not.

From the greatest to the least, they believed and turned. The king himself stepped down from his throne. Their repentance was not only words. They turned “from his evil way,” and God saw their works. And He spared them. It shows us that repentance is open to everyone, even a whole city.

application.text: Here are three steps you can take this week.
First, ask yourself honestly, “What am I carrying that I want to be free of?” Name it in prayer.
Second, make one change that matches your sorrow. Stop what needs to stop. Begin what needs to begin.
Third, if the burden is serious, speak with your bishop or branch president. He holds a key to help you through, and he will not carry you down.
Then trust the receipt. When the Savior says it is paid, it is paid.

opening.text: Any gardener will tell you the same thing. Weeds do not announce themselves. They grow quietly, a little each day. One morning you look out and the garden is full of them. You can ignore them, and they will take over. Or you can kneel down, pull them out by the root, and make room for what you want to grow.

Repentance is a lot like pulling weeds. It is humble work. It is done on our knees. But it clears the ground, and it lets good things grow. Today I want to talk about how it works and why it matters so much.

mainMessage.text: Repentance clears away what does not belong in our lives and makes room for what does. It is not a sign that we have failed. It is a sign that we are growing. Through Jesus Christ, we can start fresh again, and we can do it as often as we need.

blocks.text: The Savior’s first message in His public ministry was short and clear.
From that time Jesus began to preach, and to say, Repent: for the kingdom of heaven is at hand.
He did not begin with a long list of commands. He began with a call to turn. That is where all growth starts. Isaiah taught that when we turn, God meets us with mercy.
Let the wicked forsake his way, and the unrighteous man his thoughts: and let him return unto the Lord, and he will have mercy upon him; and to our God, for he will abundantly pardon.

Isaiah mentions our “way” and our “thoughts.” A weed pulled at the top grows back. To be rid of it, we have to deal with the root. For us, that means our thoughts and our desires, not only our actions.
Elder Dallin H. Oaks of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles spoke about this deeper change. In his talk “Repentance and Change,” from the October 2003 general conference, he said:

The gospel of Jesus Christ challenges us to change. ‘Repent’ is its most frequent message, and repenting means giving up all of our practices—personal, family, ethnic, and national—that are contrary to the commandments of God. The purpose of the gospel is to transform common creatures into celestial citizens, and that requires change.
He is not describing a quick fix. He is describing a lasting transformation. Repentance changes who we are.
Peter taught the same truth, and he named the harvest that follows.
Repent ye therefore, and be converted, that your sins may be blotted out, when the times of refreshing shall come from the presence of the Lord;
After the weeding comes the rain. “Times of refreshing” come from the Lord to a heart that has been cleared and prepared.

We can pull weeds, but we cannot make anything grow on our own. That is His work. And what He gave to make our repentance possible is beyond anything we could repay. He told Joseph Smith what it cost.
He took on Himself what we would have suffered, “if they would repent.” That little word shows that He gives us a choice. He has done His part completely. Ours is to respond.
Samuel the Lamanite spoke of this to a people who needed to hear it.

Yea, and it bringeth to pass the condition of repentance, that whosoever repenteth the same is not hewn down and cast into the fire; but whosoever repenteth not is hewn down and cast into the fire; and there cometh upon them again a spiritual death, yea, a second death, for they are cut off again as to things pertaining to righteousness.
The Savior’s sacrifice “bringeth to pass the condition of repentance.” Without Him, no amount of weeding would ever make a garden. With Him, the ground can be made new.
Elder D. Todd Christofferson of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles testified of this gift. In his talk “The Divine Gift of Repentance,” from the October 2011 general conference, he said:

I gratefully acknowledge and testify that the incomprehensible suffering, death, and Resurrection of our Lord ‘bringeth to pass the condition of repentance’ (Helaman 14:18). The divine gift of repentance is the key to happiness here and hereafter. In the Savior’s words and in deep humility and love, I invite all to ‘repent: for the kingdom of heaven is at hand’ (Matthew 4:17). I know that in accepting this invitation, you will find joy both now and forever.
He says, “I invite all.” That includes the one who feels the garden is too far gone.
What does the weeding look like? The Lord described it in a revelation given in 1831.

Behold, he who has repented of his sins, the same is forgiven, and I, the Lord, remember them no more.
By this ye may know if a man repenteth of his sins—behold, he will confess them and forsake them.

Confess means to name the weed. We say it plainly to God, and where needed, to the people we have hurt. For serious matters, we also go to our bishop or branch president. Forsake means to pull it and not plant it again. And then the great promise: “I, the Lord, remember them no more.”
Solomon wrote that hiding a weed does not stop it from growing.
He that covereth his sins shall not prosper: but whoso confesseth and forsaketh them shall have mercy.
A covered weed still grows beneath the cover. Brought into the light, it can be removed.
President Dieter F. Uchtdorf taught that this begins with trust in God. In his talk “Point of Safe Return,” from the April 2007 general conference, he said:

We need a strong faith in Christ to be able to repent. Our faith has to include a ‘correct idea of \[God’s\] character, perfections, and attributes’ (Lectures on Faith \[1985\], 38). Faith in Christ will change our thoughts, beliefs, and behaviors that are not in harmony with God’s will.
A gardener who trusts the weather keeps working. A person who trusts God’s mercy keeps turning back. That trust is what carries us.
After the weeding, the soil looks fresh and dark. Isaiah used a picture of purity to describe what the Lord does with a forgiven life.
Come now, and let us reason together, saith the Lord: though your sins be as scarlet, they shall be as white as snow; though they be red like crimson, they shall be as wool.
White as snow, soft as wool. Not patched, but made new. And note how the verse opens: “Come now, and let us reason together.” The Lord is not angry. He is inviting us into a conversation.

President Boyd K. Packer of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles spoke of how wide this promise reaches. In his talk “The Brilliant Morning of Forgiveness,” from the October 1995 general conference, he said:

The gospel teaches us that relief from torment and guilt can be earned through repentance. Save for those few who defect to perdition after having known a fulness, there is no habit, no addiction, no rebellion, no transgression, no offense exempted from the promise of complete forgiveness.
He leaves almost nothing out. If you worry that your garden is the one that cannot be cleared, this promise is for you.
The people of King Benjamin lived this. They had seen their own weeds clearly, and they pleaded for mercy.

And they had viewed themselves in their own carnal state, even less than the dust of the earth. And they all cried aloud with one voice, saying: O have mercy, and apply the atoning blood of Christ that we may receive forgiveness of our sins, and our hearts may be purified; for we believe in Jesus Christ, the Son of God, who created heaven and earth, and all things; who shall come down among the children of men.

Their cry was heard. Joy filled them, and they had peace of conscience. The ground was clear.
The Savior also told us that heaven shares this joy.
I say unto you, that likewise joy shall be in heaven over one sinner that repenteth, more than over ninety and nine just persons, which need no repentance.
When one person turns, heaven celebrates. It is not a quiet event. It is a joyful one.
Not all sorrow helps the garden. Paul taught the difference.
For godly sorrow worketh repentance to salvation not to be repented of: but the sorrow of the world worketh death.
Godly sorrow makes us want to get up and work. Worldly sorrow leaves us sitting in the weeds. Mormon saw a people with the second kind.

But behold this my joy was vain, for their sorrowing was not unto repentance, because of the goodness of God; but it was rather the sorrowing of the damned, because the Lord would not always suffer them to take happiness in sin.
They were sorry for the cost, not for the sin. That kind of sorrow produces no fruit.

And here is something every gardener knows. After you clear the ground, you still wait for growth. It does not happen overnight. Elder Neil L. Andersen of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles said the same about relief after repentance. In his talk “Repent … That I May Heal You,” from the October 2009 general conference, he said:
For those who are truly repentant but seem unable to feel relief: continue keeping the commandments. I promise you, relief will come in the timetable of the Lord. Healing also requires time.
Keep tending the garden. The commandments are the daily watering. In the Lord’s timing, the peace you hope for will come.
A good gardener does not wait for the perfect season. Amulek taught the people not to wait.

And now, as I said unto you before, as ye have had so many witnesses, therefore, I beseech of you that ye do not procrastinate the day of your repentance until the end; for after this day of life, which is given us to prepare for eternity, behold, if we do not improve our time while in this life, then cometh the night of darkness wherein there can be no labor performed.
He uses the picture of a day, then a night when no labor can be done. The time to work is now. Each day we wait, the weeds go deeper.

Elder Jeffrey R. Holland of the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles reached out to everyone who feels it is too late. In his talk “Prophets in the Land Again,” from the October 2006 general conference, he said:

To all of you who think you are lost or without hope, or who think you have done too much that was too wrong for too long, to every one of you who worry that you are stranded somewhere on the wintry plains of life and have wrecked your handcart in the process, this conference calls out Jehovah’s unrelenting refrain, ‘\[My\] hand is stretched out still’ \[see Isaiah 5:25; 9:17, 21\].
The Lord’s hand is stretched out still. Put your hand in His, and start today.

story.prompt: The member tells about a time they made a hard change and felt the result. If the member has none, the app offers a story from the scriptures.
story.title: Zacchaeus

blocks.text: Zacchaeus was a chief tax collector in Jericho. He had grown rich, and some of it, he admitted, may have been taken unfairly. When the Savior came to his house, Zacchaeus did something remarkable.

And Zacchæus stood, and said unto the Lord; Behold, Lord, the half of my goods I give to the poor; and if I have taken any thing from any man by false accusation, I restore him fourfold.
And Jesus said unto him, This day is salvation come to this house, forsomuch as he also is a son of Abraham.
For the Son of man is come to seek and to save that which was lost.

Zacchaeus did not stop at saying he was sorry. He gave half of what he owned to the poor and promised to repay anyone he had wronged four times over. That is a repentance that shows. And the Savior answered, “This day is salvation come to this house.” He came “to seek and to save that which was lost.”

application.text: Here are three things to do this week.
First, find one weed you have been ignoring. Pray about it and ask God for help to pull it up by the root.
Second, make it right where you can. Like Zacchaeus, let your repentance show in what you do.
Third, if you are carrying something serious, speak with your bishop or branch president. He is there to help you keep the garden clear.
And then give it time. What you plant today will grow.

testimony.prompt: The member adds their own words. Lines the app offers:

blocks.text: I know that God lives and that He loves each of us. I know that Jesus Christ gave Himself so that we can start again. I know that through Him, a life can be made new. I say these things in the name of Jesus Christ, amen.

invitations: I invite you to pray about one weed you have been ignoring.
I invite you to make it right where you can.
I invite you to speak with your bishop or branch president if you are carrying something serious.
blessings: You will be helped to pull it up by the root.
Your life will show your change.

closingVerse.text:
Then said he to the multitude that came forth to be baptized of him, O generation of vipers, who hath warned you to flee from the wrath to come?
Bring forth therefore fruits worthy of repentance, and begin not to say within yourselves, We have Abraham to our father: for I say unto you, That God is able of these stones to raise up children unto Abraham.

leaderQuotes.Talk title: Repent … That I May Heal You
